posts.caption: The show bill said ring four, ten-fifteen, so we arrived at eight and sat in the trailer eating gas station donuts. She was braided by nine, which is a record for both of us. At ten-fifteen she walked into the ring like she owned the lease. The scores came back by noon and I read them in the truck with the engine off. She spent the drive home with her nose against the feed bin, perfectly at peace. I framed the ribbon anyway. It's by the sink with the peppermints.
posts.first: My mother kept every ribbon she ever won in a shoebox under the bed. Mine are on a pegboard in the tack room, mostly the pale colors. The pale ones hang next to the good ones and nobody has ever asked me to sort them.

posts.caption: Every barn has a horse who retires without ever being told. Ours did it on a Tuesday in March, when he stopped following the others to the far fence and started standing by the water trough instead. Nobody scheduled a party. We just moved his hay net closer to the gate and he took it as a promotion. These days he spends the mornings supervising the young ones from a comfortable distance. He's never once offered advice. He just keeps standing there, and somehow they settle down.
posts.first: My first horse lived to thirty-one. In his last summer he stopped bothering with the fence line and just stood by the gate for hours. I stood with him most evenings after work. I never thought of it as time I was giving up.

posts.quote: He's walked past that blue barrel for nine years. Today it's a threat. Nobody knows what changed, least of all the barrel.
posts.first: Last fall I moved a blue barrel three feet to the left to sweep behind it. The horse noticed at once and kept an eye on it for a week. I eventually put it back. He walked past like nothing had happened, and I've never mentioned it either.

posts.caption: The farrier's name is Dale and he drives a white truck with a rattle that I can hear from the kitchen. He has been coming every six weeks for eleven years. In that time I have never once forgotten the appointment, and I have never once been ready for it. This morning I filled the hay nets at six, swept the aisle twice, and found a clean towel for his stand. The horse watched all of it from her stall with deep suspicion. At seven fifty-eight the rattle started up the drive.
posts.first: Dale once told me the best thing a horse owner can do is stand back and drink coffee. I took it as advice for years. It turns out he just wanted me out of the aisle. The coffee is still excellent, though.

posts.caption: The new boarder showed up on a Saturday with a very clean trailer and a lot of questions. By Sunday she had learned which gate sticks, which bucket belongs to nobody, and which stall has the good window. Nobody told her. She worked it out by watching. Our barn has a quiet system that none of us has ever written down. Every few years someone new tries to figure out how it works, and every few years we let them think they did.
posts.first: When I first boarded here, the woman who ran the barn told me I would find my place. Nobody explained. Three weeks later somebody moved my bucket to the end of the row, and I understood. I still keep it there. It has a good view of the door.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a huge copper draft mare with feathered legs, round glasses and a patterned blanket, lifting one hoof in a sunset pasture while an orange barn cat on a fence post stares back at her. Text at the top reads: The new boarder asked who runs this barn. Text at the bottom reads: The barn cat and I looked at each other. It's complicated.

posts.caption: I fill the wheelbarrow every morning at six and park it in the aisle while I haul water. It takes about four minutes, which is apparently plenty. Last Tuesday I came back to find it on its side, the manure fork across the aisle, and Pudding standing next to it with straw in his forelock. He looked at me the way a man looks at a lawn he just finished mowing. I righted the wheelbarrow and started over. He followed me down the aisle the whole way, close enough to supervise and not close enough to be asked to help.
posts.first: My father had a wheelbarrow he called the old reliable. It lasted thirty years and never once tipped over on its own. Ours has lasted two months. I keep it by the door now with a bucket of grain on the seat, and so far that works about half the time.
